summary:
Darksight (https://darksight.space) is Team GLYFT's entry for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 "Lunar Landing Site Navigator". It is a free website for mission planners and curious minds to pick lunar landing sites and dates and see, side by side, when each site gets sunlight for power and when it can see Earth for radio.

What we built: The Sun and Earth positions come from NASA JPL's DE440 data, every 3 hours from 1900 to 2100, and match JPL Horizons to within 0.1°. Near the south pole, each site's skyline is worked out from LOLA height data up to 150 km away, so crater rims and peaks cast real shadows. Up to three sites can be pinned and compared in a table. It shows how long until sunset and until Earth drops below the skyline, the share of time in sunlight, and the longest dark period. There is also a timeline, a sky panorama and a 3D view of the terrain. "Nudge" buttons show what moving 1 km or waiting a day changes. Extra tools include map layers for the whole Moon, a battery model, a date search, a landing simulation and a printable mission report.

Why it matters: The lunar south pole is where the Artemis landings are planned. There the Sun stays close to the horizon, so a few hundred metres can mean the difference between near-constant light and permanent shadow. Darksight shows these power and radio trade-offs in seconds, without specialist software.
details:
What it does

Darksight is a free website for choosing where and when to land on the Moon. You pick a site by clicking the map, choosing one of 24 curated sites, or typing coordinates. Then you pick any time between 1900 and 2100. Darksight tells you whether that site has sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for radio, measured against the real terrain skyline.

It shows countdowns such as "Sunset in 47 d 18 h" or "Permanently shadowed (until 2100)". You can pin up to three scenarios and compare them side by side. The comparison covers the share of the next 30 days in sunlight and in contact with Earth, the longest dark period and the longest gap in contact, with the best value in each row marked.

A nudge tool moves the site by 1 km or the date by one day and says in words what changes. At the south pole, moving just 1 km north of Shackleton crater's rim loses 17 of the next 30 days of sunlight.

How it works

Python prepares the data once. It builds a table of the Sun's and Earth's directions as seen from the Moon, every 3 hours from 1900 to 2100, using NASA JPL's DE440 ephemeris. It also processes NASA's LRO LOLA height maps of the lunar surface.

The key idea is that at any moment the Sun and Earth are in the same direction for every site on the Moon. Only each site's local "up" differs. So one small table serves every site, and the browser works out the rest: the angles, the terrain skyline traced 150 km out in every direction, and the rise and set times. The site is static files only, with no server, database or accounts.

Benefits

Today a planner needs about an hour across three separate tools to check one site and date. Darksight answers it in seconds and lets you compare several options at once. Because of the nudge tool, "what if we land a kilometre off, or launch a day late?" becomes a one-click question.

The results can be trusted. We compared our angles with NASA JPL Horizons in 18 test cases. The largest difference was 0.000001°, and that figure is shown on every page. The project has 785 automated tests, and the site lists its own limits openly.

It runs on desktops and phones, and a share link reopens the exact same comparison.

Intended impact

We want mission planners to shortlist landing sites and dates by power and radio before they start detailed analysis. We also want students, educators and curious people to see why the lunar south pole is so promising and so unforgiving. There, the Sun skims the horizon, and a single ridge can hide it for days.

Tools, languages and software

The website is written in TypeScript and built with Vite. It uses three.js for the 3D view and Plotly.js for the charts. Data preparation uses Python with Skyfield, NumPy and Pillow. Testing uses Vitest and Playwright, and GitHub Actions and Cloudflare Pages build and host the site.

The data comes from NASA's LRO LOLA height maps and illumination maps, the JPL DE440 ephemeris and the JPL Horizons API. No special hardware was needed beyond our laptops.

The team used AI coding assistants, mainly Claude Code. Every AI-generated piece was checked by a team member and recorded publicly in the repo.

How it's creative

Existing tools look at one site at one moment. Darksight is built around comparison and sensitivity: it shows how much the answer changes when the plan changes slightly.

The single shared table of Sun and Earth directions is a simple trick. It lets a whole Moon's worth of calculations run in a web browser with no server.

The same answer is shown several ways: a timeline, a sky panorama with the real skyline, a 2D map and a 3D scene where the Sun lights the actual terrain. It also includes a flight planner from an Earth launch pad to touchdown at the chosen site and time.

Factors the team considered

Accuracy came first. Every number shown to the user comes from one tested calculation module and is checked against NASA's own tools. We used real physics, so no atmospheric refraction is applied, because the Moon has no atmosphere.

We were honest about data limits. The best height map covers only the south pole, so coarser global data fills in the rest of the Moon, and the page always says which source applies.

We also designed for accessibility, with a colour-blind-safe palette and readable contrast. The site works on phones and needs no accounts. Finally, we credited every data source and documented how AI was used.
